title: Multi-tenant noise and CUDA-version crosswalk for latency stability
content:
Purpose:
This note documents an experiment and analysis that explores how multi-tenant GPU noise interacts with CUDA/driver versions across A100, H100 and L40S SKUs. Our goal is to identify concrete sources of p95/p99 latency jitter that appear only when (a) background best-effort tenants are present and (b) there is variation in CUDA+driver stacks across hosts. We aim to provide short-term mitigations and longer-term runtime guardrails (pinning recommendations, scheduling constraints, and runtime telemetry changes).

Background and motivation:
Operational incidents over the last two quarters showed sporadic p99 spikes (~20–60ms extra) on hosted clusters serving medium-context chat workloads. The spikes correlated with periods of high best-effort batch activity and driver rollouts in specific regions. Prior SKU-level studies (see linked artifacts) focused on single-tenant microbenchmarks. This study purposefully runs mixed-tenant workloads + multiple driver/CUDA stacks to observe real-world interference and kernel fallback behavior.

Hypotheses tested:
- H1: Driver/CUDA mismatch across hosts increases kernel launch variability under multi-tenant interference (due to different kernel selection paths).
- H2: L40S exhibits different tail-behavior than A100/H100 when host-side preemption from other processes occurs because of slower preemption paths in the L40S firmware/driver.
- H3: Background contention (PCIe/NVLink, host memory bandwidth) is the dominant contributor to p99 under multi-tenant noise, with driver differences amplifying tail effects but not changing median.

Experiment design:
- SKUs: NVIDIA A100 40GB (GCP and AWS variants), H100 80GB (GCP/Oracle variants), L40S 48GB (AWS variant).
- CUDA versions tested: 11.8, 12.1, 12.2. Driver versions tested: 525.x, 535.x, 545.x (combinations that customers might have pinned).
- Tenancy scenarios: (1) Single-tenant baseline (isolated inference process), (2) Controlled multi-tenant — one inference process + synthetic best-effort batch worker generating memory copies and small kernels to simulate other tenants at 40% GPU utilization, (3) Aggressive multi-tenant — 2 additional tenants with bursty kernels and frequent large host-to-device transfers.
- Workloads: medium-context decoder-only model (˜13B parameters), prompt lengths 64 prefills + 256 decode, batch sizes: single request, and 4 concurrent requests. Common runtime config used: continuous batching disabled for clarity, KV cache warm for reuse measurements.
- Measurements: token-level p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU SM utilization, PCIe/NVLink link utilization (where exposed), CUDA kernel timings (nvprof-style), kernel fallback counts, and driver-level warnings from dmesg. Each test ran for 90 minutes to capture rolling noise and maintenance-like events.

Key observations (summary):
1) Baseline differences: median latencies across SKUs were within expected deltas (A100 slightly faster p50 than L40S; H100 fastest for long-context operations). None of the baselines showed pathological tail behavior by themselves.
2) Multi-tenant tail amplification: adding a single best-effort tenant produced modest p95 increases (5–12%). However, p99 increased dramatically in some CUDA/driver combos (up to +45ms) primarily on H100 hosts running CUDA 12.2 + driver 545.x.
3) Driver+CUDA interaction: the most consistent tail amplification correlated with combinations where the driver chose a different optimized kernel path under high memory copy pressure. We observed kernel re-compilation/fallback-like messages and longer kernel queue waits in those host logs. H100 showed this most clearly — some kernels moved from a tensor-core optimized path to a non-tensor path under contention leading to ~8–12% per-token decode latency on bursts.
4) L40S behavior: L40S experienced smaller proportional p99 deltas for single best-effort tenants but showed a different symptom under aggressive multi-tenancy: longer run-to-run variability (p99 spikes were rarer but when occurred, lasted longer — 10–20 minutes). dmesg showed repeated host-side preemption entries on L40S nodes during those windows.
5) PCIe/NVLink pressure: when we saturated host-device transfers (simulating NVMe→GPU streaming for other tenants), hosts with NVLink topology (multi-GPU) amplified local interference because driver scheduling serialized some DMA paths; this affected multi-GPU placement decisions and increased tail latency by 5–20% depending on topology.
6) No single source dominant: both host-side memory bandwidth contention and driver kernel-path variation matter. The dominant cause varied by SKU and driver combination.

Representative numbers (aggregated across runs):
- A100 (CUDA 12.1, driver 535): baseline p99 = 280ms; controlled multi-tenant p99 = 330ms (+18%); aggressive = 395ms (+41%).
- H100 (CUDA 12.2, driver 545): baseline p99 = 210ms; controlled multi-tenant p99 = 255ms (+21%); aggressive p99 = 335ms (+59%).
- L40S (CUDA 11.8, driver 525): baseline p99 = 300ms; controlled multi-tenant p99 = 340ms (+13%); aggressive p99 = 380ms (+27%), with longer-duration spikes observed in tail windows.

Logs and kernel-level evidence:
- We captured kernel timing histograms showing a class of GEMM kernels with bimodal distributions on H100 under driver 545.x when background DMA was present. The longer-mode matched to fallback to a slower kernel path (confirmed by inspecting kernel names and driver tracepoints).
- dmesg on L40S hosts recorded repeated "GPU preemption" messages coincident with the long-duration p99 spikes.

Operational recommendations (short-term):
- Pin production H100 fleets to CUDA 12.1 + driver 535.x (the combination with the most stable tail behaviour under our workloads). Avoid CUDA 12.2 + driver 545.x until further kernel-selection analysis is completed.
- For L40S clusters supporting mixed tenant types, prefer instance-level soft-isolation during rollout windows: schedule best-effort batch tenants on separate host pools during business hours to reduce long-duration spikes.
- Add a preflight check in rollout automation that runs a short mixed-tenant microbench (10 minutes) to detect kernel-path regressions for a driver->CUDA combo before fleet-wide rollout.
- Increase runtime telemetry: emit kernel-path fingerprints (kernel names and durations) at p95/p99 intervals to detect bimodal GEMM behaviors sooner.

Longer-term changes and engineering follow-ups:
- Runtime: implement a lightweight kernel-path cache and a compatibility check that prefers stable kernel code paths for serving workloads (consider forcing a particular kernel path when detected as producing lower tail latency).
- Scheduler: add tenancy-awareness when placing inference-only low-latency pods — prefer node pools with matching CUDA/driver stacks for critical customers.
- Testing: expand CI to include mixed-tenant interference tests that run across CUDA/driver matrices and produce telemetry summaries for each PR that modifies the kernel selection code.

Open questions and next experiments:
- Is the bimodal kernel behavior reproducible with microbenchmarks only targeting GEMM kernels, or is it an emergent property of full model graphs + DMA contention? We need a focused microbench with identical tensor shapes run under background DMA to confirm.
- Can driver-level knobs (e.g. CUDA UVM throttling parameters, preemption policy) reduce the long-duration spikes on L40S without sacrificing throughput?

Appendix: brief runbook for rollout pinning (for SRE/product ops)
- When provisioning new H100 capacity: set image to CUDA 12.1 / driver 535.x; add label gpu.stack=12.1-535 for scheduler bin-packing.
- If a driver upgrade is required: run staged rollout: 5% canary (run mixed-tenant microbench), 25% ramp (monitor kernel-path telemetry), then full rollout. Abort if p99 tail increases >15% vs baseline for two consecutive 10-minute windows.
- For L40S: avoid colocating best-effort NVMe→GPU streaming tenants with latency-sensitive serving pods in the same AZ during peak windows.

Notes and caveats:
- These results are workload-sensitive (13B, medium-context). Smaller models and purely stateless short-context scenarios will show smaller absolute deltas but can still reveal bimodal kernel path issues under heavy background DMA.
- Cloud provider firmware differences (firmware versions for GPUs, NIC drivers) can change outcomes; cross-cloud reproducibility must always check firmware+driver+CUDA triple.

Conclusion:
Mixed-tenant noise and CUDA/driver variations produce non-linear amplification of tail latency. H100 in our tests was the most sensitive to kernel-path variation under CUDA 12.2 + 545.x, whereas L40S showed longer duration spikes likely tied to preemption behavior. Operational mitigations (stack pinning, isolation pools, rollout microbench checks) are effective immediate levers while runtime and scheduler-level mitigations are developed.
